prompt: What does it mean for two operators Â and B̂ to commute?

choices.text: Applying Â then B̂ gives the same result as B̂ then Â
Applying Â and then B̂ to any function always gives zero
choices.why: It is the difference ÂB̂ − B̂Â that is zero, not the result of applying them. Commuting means both orders give the same result.

choices.text: Each of the two operators leaves every function unchanged
choices.why: Commuting operators can change a function; they just change it the same way in either order.

choices.text: Â and B̂ are really the same operator, written twice
choices.why: Different operators can commute: multiplying by 3x and multiplying by x^−1 do, for example. Commuting means the order doesn't matter.

explanation: Two operators commute when the order in which they act doesn't matter: ÂB̂f(x) = B̂Âf(x) for any function f(x). Equivalently, their commutator [Â, B̂] = ÂB̂ − B̂Â is zero.

prompt: Which expression is the commutator [Â, B̂]?

choices.text: ÂB̂ − B̂Â
ÂB̂ + B̂Â
choices.why: The commutator subtracts the two orders, so that it is zero when they agree: [Â, B̂] = ÂB̂ − B̂Â.

choices.text: Â − B̂
choices.why: The commutator compares the two orders of applying both operators, ÂB̂ and B̂Â, not the operators on their own.

choices.text: ÂB̂
choices.why: ÂB̂ is just one order. The commutator is the difference between the two orders, ÂB̂ − B̂Â.

explanation: The commutator is [Â, B̂] = ÂB̂ − B̂Â. If it equals zero, the two orders give the same result and the operators commute.

prompt: To test whether Â and B̂ commute, you apply ÂB̂ to a function f(x), apply B̂Â to the same f(x), and subtract. Which result shows that they commute?

choices.text: Zero, whatever f(x) is
A constant times f(x)
choices.why: A nonzero result, even a constant times f(x), means the two orders differ, so the operators do not commute.

choices.text: The function f(x) itself
choices.why: If the difference were f(x), the two orders would differ by f(x). They commute only when the difference is zero.

choices.text: 1, for any function f(x)
choices.why: A difference of 1 would mean the two orders give different results. They commute only if the difference is zero.

explanation: If ÂB̂f(x) and B̂Âf(x) are the same, subtracting them gives zero, so [Â, B̂] = 0 and the operators commute. Any other result means the order matters.

prompt: In general, does the order in which two operators act on a function matter?

choices.text: Yes, unless the two operators commute
No, operators can always be swapped like numbers
choices.why: Operators are not just numbers. For example, d/dx and x^2 give different results in different orders.

choices.text: Only if one of the operators contains ħ
choices.why: d/dx and x^2 contain no ħ, yet they do not commute. What matters is whether the two orders give the same result.

choices.text: Only if one of the operators is a constant
choices.why: It's the other way round: multiplying by a constant, like Î = 5, commutes with the operators in this section. Order matters for pairs like d/dx and x^2.

explanation: One important property of operators is that the order of operation matters: in general ÂB̂f(x) ≠ B̂Âf(x). The two orders give the same result only when the operators commute.

prompt: In the expression Â{Êf(x)}, which operator acts on f(x) first?

choices.text: Ê, the operator written next to f(x)
Â, the operator written on the left
choices.why: Â acts on whatever Ê produces, so it acts second. In Example 4.6.1a, Â{Êf(x)} = Â{x^2 f(x)}: Ê multiplies by x^2 first.

choices.text: Both act on f(x) at the same moment
choices.why: Operators act one after the other. The one next to f(x), Ê, acts first, and Â acts on its result.

choices.text: Whichever of the two operators is simpler
choices.why: The order is set by how the expression is written, not by which operator is simpler: the one next to f(x) acts first.

explanation: The operator nearest the function acts first. In Example 4.6.1a, Â{Êf(x)} = Â{x^2 f(x)} = d/dx{x^2 f(x)}: Ê (multiply by x^2) acts first, and Â (d/dx) acts on the result.

prompt: Which pair of everyday operations does the section use as an example of operations that commute?

choices.text: Brushing your teeth and combing your hair
Getting dressed and taking a shower
choices.why: The section gives this as a pair that does not commute: showering and then dressing is not the same as dressing and then showering.

choices.text: Putting on your socks and putting on your shoes
choices.why: Here the order matters: with your shoes on first, you can't put your socks on underneath. Commuting operations give the same result in either order.

choices.text: Cracking an egg and frying it
choices.why: You can't fry an egg before cracking it, so the order matters. The section's commuting pair is brushing your teeth and combing your hair.

explanation: Brushing your teeth and combing your hair commute: doing them in either order gives the same result. Getting dressed and taking a shower do not, because the outcome depends on which you do first.

prompt: If the operators for two physical quantities commute, what does that mean for measuring the quantities?

choices.text: Both can be measured at the same time with no limit on precision
Only one of them can be measured at a time
choices.why: That is closer to what happens when operators do not commute. Commuting operators let both be measured together exactly.

choices.text: Both can be measured together, but never more precisely than ħ/2
choices.why: ħ/2 is the limit for position and momentum, which do not commute. Commuting quantities have no such limit.

choices.text: Neither of them can ever be measured exactly
choices.why: Commuting is the good case: both quantities can be measured exactly, at the same time.

explanation: If two operators commute, the corresponding physical quantities can be measured simultaneously to any precision, with no limit on the uncertainty. That is what the section's title means by infinite precision.

prompt: If two operators do not commute, what happens when you try to measure both quantities at the same time?

choices.text: Measuring one more precisely makes the other less precise
Both can still be measured exactly with good enough instruments
choices.why: This limit is not about instruments. Operators that do not commute force a tradeoff in precision between the two quantities.

choices.text: The two quantities are forced to have the same value
choices.why: Non-commuting operators do not make the values equal; they limit how precisely both can be known together.

choices.text: Neither quantity can be measured at all
choices.why: Each quantity can be measured. What's limited is how precisely both can be known at the same time.

explanation: If two operators do not commute, there is a tradeoff: the more precisely one quantity is measured, the less precisely the other can be known. This is the Heisenberg uncertainty principle.

prompt: According to the section, which principle do the commutation relations of operators represent mathematically?

choices.text: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle
The Pauli exclusion principle
choices.why: The Pauli principle is about electrons sharing a state. Commutators tell you which quantities can be known precisely together: the uncertainty principle.

choices.text: Planck's quantization of energy
choices.why: Planck's idea is that energy comes in quanta of hν. Commutators are linked to the uncertainty principle.

choices.text: The conservation of energy
choices.why: Commutators say nothing about conserving energy. They express the uncertainty principle: whether two quantities can be known precisely at once.

explanation: Whether two operators commute decides whether both quantities can be measured at once with infinite precision, or only with a tradeoff. This is the mathematical form of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle.

prompt: What can two operators that commute have in common?

choices.text: The same set of eigenfunctions
The same eigenvalue for every eigenfunction
choices.why: The eigenfunctions can be shared, but the eigenvalues can differ: Âψ = aψ and B̂ψ = bψ, with a and b different numbers.

choices.text: A commutator equal to iħ
choices.why: A commutator of iħ means two operators do not commute, as for position and momentum. Commuting operators have a commutator of zero.

choices.text: Neither of them can have any eigenfunctions
choices.why: Commuting operators do have eigenfunctions; in fact they can share the same set.

explanation: If two operators commute, they can have the same set of eigenfunctions. Then a state can have exact values of both quantities at once, so both can be measured simultaneously.

prompt: Â and B̂ commute, and ψ is an eigenfunction of B̂ with eigenvalue b. The section shows that B̂(Âψ) = b(Âψ). What does this tell you about Âψ?

choices.text: An eigenfunction of B̂ with the same eigenvalue b
An eigenfunction of B̂ with eigenvalue −b instead
choices.why: The equation B̂(Âψ) = b(Âψ) has b, not −b, on the right: the eigenvalue is unchanged.

choices.text: Zero, whatever the function ψ is
choices.why: The equation does not force Âψ to be zero. It shows Âψ is an eigenfunction of B̂ with eigenvalue b, so at most Â multiplies ψ by a constant.

choices.text: A new function with nothing to do with ψ
choices.why: Since Âψ has the same eigenvalue b as ψ, Â cannot turn ψ into a different function; at most it multiplies ψ by a constant.

explanation: B̂(Âψ) = b(Âψ) says Âψ is an eigenfunction of B̂ with eigenvalue b. So Â cannot change ψ: at most it multiplies ψ by a constant, Âψ = aψ, which makes ψ an eigenfunction of Â as well.

prompt: Â and B̂ commute, and ψ is an eigenfunction of both, with Âψ = 2ψ and B̂ψ = 3ψ. B̂(Âψ) equals some number times ψ. What is that number?
explanation: B̂(Âψ) = B̂(2ψ) = 2B̂ψ = 2 × 3ψ = 6ψ, so the number is ab = 2 × 3 = 6. The other order, Â(B̂ψ) = Â(3ψ) = 3 × 2ψ = 6ψ, gives the same result, as it must for commuting operators.

prompt: A system is in a state ψ that is an eigenfunction of two commuting operators, with Âψ = aψ and B̂ψ = bψ. What do measurements of the two quantities give?

choices.text: Exactly a for the first and exactly b for the second
Exactly a for the first, but an uncertain value for the second
choices.why: ψ is an eigenfunction of B̂ too, so B also has the exact value b. Commuting quantities can both be known exactly.

choices.text: The product ab for both quantities
choices.why: ab appears when you apply both operators, B̂(Âψ) = abψ, but each measurement gives its own operator's eigenvalue: a or b.

choices.text: The average of a and b for both quantities
choices.why: Each operator has its own eigenvalue, and the measured values are the eigenvalues, so the results are a and b.

explanation: The eigenvalues of an operator are the values that are measured. Because ψ is an eigenfunction of both commuting operators, A has the exact value a and B the exact value b at the same time.

prompt: In Example 4.6.1a, do Â = d/dx and Ê = x^2 commute?

choices.text: No; [Â, Ê]f(x) = 2x f(x), which is not zero
Yes; both orders give the same result, x^2 f'(x)
choices.why: Only d/dx first gives x^2 f'(x). Multiplying by x^2 first and then differentiating gives 2x f(x) + x^2 f'(x).

choices.text: Yes; the commutator [Â, Ê] is zero for every f(x)
choices.why: Subtracting the two orders leaves 2x f(x), which is not zero, so they do not commute.

choices.text: No; [Â, Ê]f(x) = x^2 f'(x), which is not zero
choices.why: x^2 f'(x) is the term both orders share, and it cancels in the subtraction. What is left over is 2x f(x).

explanation: Â{Êf(x)} = d/dx{x^2 f(x)} = 2x f(x) + x^2 f'(x) by the product rule, while Ê{Âf(x)} = x^2 f'(x). The difference is 2x f(x) ≠ 0, so d/dx and x^2 do not commute.

prompt: In Example 4.6.1a, what do you get if you first take the derivative of f(x) and then multiply by x^2?

choices.text: 2x f(x) + x^2 f'(x)
choices.why: That is the other order: multiply by x^2 first, then take the derivative, which by the product rule adds 2x f(x).

choices.text: 2x f(x)
choices.why: 2x f(x) is the commutator, the difference between the two orders, not the result of one order.

choices.text: x^2 f(x)
choices.why: That skips the derivative. Taking d/dx first gives f'(x), and multiplying by x^2 then gives x^2 f'(x).

explanation: Ê{Âf(x)} = Ê{f'(x)} = x^2 f'(x). The other order, d/dx{x^2 f(x)}, gives an extra 2x f(x) from the product rule, which is why the two operators do not commute.

prompt: In Example 4.6.1b, B̂ multiplies a function by h/x and Ĉ adds 3 to it. Why don't they commute?

choices.text: Adding 3 first means the 3 is multiplied by h/x as well
Because h is Planck's constant, and constants never commute
choices.why: Multiplying by a constant commutes with many operators, as Î = 5 does in Example 4.6.2B. The trouble is the order of multiplying and adding.

choices.text: Because Ĉ takes a derivative of the function
choices.why: Ĉ only adds 3; there is no derivative. The order matters because the 3 gets multiplied by h/x only if it is added first.

choices.text: Because Ĉ shifts the variable from x to x + 3
choices.why: Ĉ adds 3 to the value of the function, giving f(x) + 3; it doesn't shift x. The order matters because the 3 gets multiplied by h/x only if it is added first.

explanation: B̂{Ĉf(x)} = (h/x)(f(x) + 3) = (hf(x))/x + (3h)/x, while Ĉ{B̂f(x)} = (hf(x))/x + 3. Adding 3 before multiplying lets the 3 be multiplied by h/x too, so the results differ and the operators do not commute.

prompt: As in Example 4.6.1b, Ĉ adds 3 to a function: Ĉ{f(x)} = f(x) + 3. Let B̂ double a function: B̂{f(x)} = 2f(x). For f(x) = 1, what is B̂{Ĉf(x)} − Ĉ{B̂f(x)}?
explanation: Adding 3 first and then doubling gives B̂{Ĉf(x)} = 2 × (1 + 3) = 8. Doubling first and then adding 3 gives Ĉ{B̂f(x)} = 2 × 1 + 3 = 5. The difference is 8 − 5 = 3, not zero, so B̂ and Ĉ do not commute: the added 3 gets doubled only when it is added first.

prompt: Which pair of operators commutes?

choices.text: Multiplying by 3x and multiplying by x^−1
d/dx and multiplying by x^2
choices.why: Example 4.6.1a shows these do not commute: their commutator gives 2x f(x).

choices.text: Multiplying by h/x and adding 3
choices.why: Example 4.6.1b shows these do not commute: adding 3 first lets the 3 be multiplied by h/x too.

choices.text: The position operator x̂ and the momentum operator p̂
choices.why: Their commutator is iħ, not zero, so position and momentum do not commute.

explanation: In Example 4.6.1c, both orders just multiply f(x) by 3x and by x^−1, giving 3f(x) either way, so [Ĵ, Ô] = 0. Ordinary multiplication doesn't depend on order.

prompt: In Example 4.6.1c, Ĵ multiplies a function by 3x and Ô multiplies it by x^−1. Applied one after the other, in either order, they multiply f(x) by what number?
explanation: Either way, f(x) is multiplied by 3x and by x^−1: 3x × x^−1 × f(x) = 3f(x). Both orders give 3f(x), so [Ĵ, Ô] = 3f(x) − 3f(x) = 0 and the operators commute.

prompt: Î multiplies a function by 5, and Â = d/dx. For f(x) = e^(2x), Â{Îf(x)} = d/dx(5e^(2x)) is some number times e^(2x). What is that number?
explanation: d/dx(5e^(2x)) = 5 × 2e^(2x) = 10e^(2x). The other order gives the same: Î{Âf(x)} = 5 × 2e^(2x) = 10e^(2x). A constant factor comes straight out of a derivative, so multiplying by a constant commutes with d/dx.

prompt: In Example 4.6.2B, why does Î, which multiplies a function by 5, commute with L̂, an integral from 1 to ∞?

choices.text: A constant factor of 5 can be taken in or out of the integral
Every integral from 1 to ∞ is equal to zero
choices.why: The integral isn't zero in general. The two terms of the commutator cancel because the 5 can be moved through the integral.

choices.text: Î leaves every function unchanged
choices.why: Î = 5 multiplies a function by 5, so it does change it. It commutes because a constant comes out of an integral.

choices.text: L̂ is a derivative, and derivatives commute with everything
choices.why: L̂ is an integral, and derivatives don't commute with everything: d/dx and x^2 do not commute.

explanation: [Î, L̂]f(x) = 5∫_1^(∞) f(x) dx − ∫_1^(∞) 5f(x) dx = 0, because a constant can be taken outside an integral. Multiplying by 5 before or after integrating gives the same result.

prompt: In the general uncertainty relation σ_A σ_B ≥ (1/2)|∫ψ^*[ÂB̂ − B̂Â]ψ dτ|, what are σ_A and σ_B?

choices.text: The uncertainties in the two quantities
The eigenvalues a and b of the two operators
choices.why: Eigenvalues are the measured values themselves. σ_A and σ_B measure how uncertain those values are.

choices.text: The two operators Â and B̂ themselves
choices.why: The operators appear inside the integral. σ_A and σ_B are numbers: the standard deviations of the measured values.

choices.text: The probabilities of measuring a and b
choices.why: σ_A and σ_B are not probabilities; they are standard deviations, the spread in the measured values.

explanation: σ_A and σ_B are the uncertainties, or standard deviations, in the physical quantities associated with Â and B̂. The relation says their product can't be smaller than the right-hand side.

prompt: If Â and B̂ commute, what is the right-hand side of the general uncertainty relation, σ_A σ_B ≥ (1/2)|∫ψ^*[ÂB̂ − B̂Â]ψ dτ|?

choices.text: Zero, so there is no limit on the uncertainties
ħ/2, just as for position and momentum
choices.why: ħ/2 comes from [x̂, p̂] = iħ. For commuting operators ÂB̂ − B̂Â = 0, so the right-hand side is zero.

choices.text: Infinity, so neither quantity can be known
choices.why: Commuting makes the bracket ÂB̂ − B̂Â zero, so the right-hand side is zero, not infinite.

choices.text: 1, so the uncertainties multiply to at least 1
choices.why: The bracket is the commutator, which is zero for commuting operators, so the right-hand side is zero.

explanation: If Â and B̂ commute, ÂB̂ − B̂Â = 0, so the right-hand side is zero. Either or both of σ_A and σ_B can then be zero: there is no restriction on measuring the eigenvalues a and b.

prompt: Â and B̂ do not commute, and the quantity A is known exactly, so σ_A = 0. What does the section say about σ_B?

choices.text: It must be infinite
It must be zero too
choices.why: Both can be zero only for commuting operators. Here σ_A σ_B has a nonzero lower limit, so σ_B must be infinite.

choices.text: It must equal exactly ħ/2
choices.why: ħ/2 is a limit on the product σ_x σ_px for position and momentum. With σ_A = 0, the product can't reach a nonzero limit unless σ_B is infinite.

choices.text: It can take any value
choices.why: For non-commuting operators the product σ_A σ_B has a nonzero lower limit, so with σ_A = 0, σ_B can't be finite.

explanation: If Â and B̂ do not commute, the right-hand side is not zero, so neither σ_A nor σ_B can be zero unless the other is infinite. Knowing A exactly means knowing nothing about B.

prompt: What does the commutator of position and momentum in one dimension, [x̂, p̂], equal?

choices.text: iħ

choices.why: A zero commutator would let position and momentum be known exactly together. They do not commute: [x̂, p̂] = iħ.
ħ/2 is the lower limit on σ_x σ_px that the commutator leads to, not the commutator itself.

choices.text: ħ
choices.why: The commutator has a factor of i: [x̂, p̂] = iħ.

explanation: Exercise 4.6.1 shows that [x̂, p̂] = x̂p̂ − p̂x̂ = iħ. Because this is not zero, position and momentum cannot both be measured to arbitrary precision at the same time.

prompt: Given that [x̂, p̂] = x̂p̂ − p̂x̂ = iħ, what is [p̂, x̂]?

choices.text: −iħ
iħ
choices.why: Swapping the order swaps the two terms: [p̂, x̂] = p̂x̂ − x̂p̂, which is minus [x̂, p̂].
Reversing the order of the operators doesn't make them commute; it only changes the sign of the commutator.
Swapping the order doesn't invert the commutator; it just changes its sign: [p̂, x̂] = −[x̂, p̂].

explanation: [p̂, x̂] = p̂x̂ − x̂p̂ = −(x̂p̂ − p̂x̂) = −iħ. The uncertainty relation uses the absolute value, so the bound is ħ/2 either way.

prompt: Using [x̂, p̂] = iħ in the general uncertainty relation, what lower limit does the section find for σ_x σ_px?

choices.why: A lower limit of 0 would mean no restriction, which happens only for commuting operators. Here the limit is ħ/2.

choices.text: iħ
choices.why: Uncertainties are real, positive numbers. The relation takes (1/2) times the absolute value of iħ, which gives ħ/2.

choices.text: 2ħ
choices.why: The relation has a factor of 1/2, not 2: (1/2)|iħ| = ħ/2.

explanation: For position and momentum the right-hand side of σ_A σ_B ≥ (1/2)|∫ψ^*[ÂB̂ − B̂Â]ψ dτ| becomes (1/2)|iħ| = ħ/2, so σ_x σ_px ≥ ħ/2.

prompt: Use σ_x σ_px ≥ ħ/2 with ħ = 1.055 × 10^−34 J·s. A particle's position has an uncertainty σ_x = 2.0 × 10^−10 m. What is the smallest possible uncertainty in its momentum, σ_px, in kg·m/s? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e-25.)
explanation: σ_px ≥ ħ/(2σ_x) = (1.055 × 10^−34 J·s)/(2 × 2.0 × 10^−10 m) = 2.64 × 10^−25 kg·m/s. Because x̂ and p̂ do not commute, a smaller σ_x would force a larger σ_px.

prompt: According to the section, which angular momentum quantities can be known exactly at the same time?

choices.text: The magnitude and one component, usually z
All three components, L_x, L_y and L_z
choices.why: The components do not commute with each other, for example [L̂_x, L̂_y] = iħL̂_z, so they can't all be known at once.

choices.text: The magnitude and all three of its components
choices.why: L̂^2 commutes with each component, but the components don't commute with each other, so only one component can be known along with the magnitude.

choices.text: Only one component, and never the magnitude
choices.why: L̂^2 commutes with each component, so the magnitude can be known together with one component.

explanation: L̂^2 commutes with L̂_x, L̂_y and L̂_z, but the components do not commute with each other. So the magnitude and one component, usually z, can be known together, and nothing is known about the other two.

prompt: What does the section give for the commutator [L̂_x, L̂_y] of two angular momentum components?

choices.text: iħL̂_z

choices.why: A zero commutator would mean L̂_x and L̂_y commute. The components of angular momentum do not commute with each other.
L̂^2 is the square of the magnitude, which commutes with each component. The commutator of L̂_x and L̂_y is iħL̂_z.

choices.text: iħ
choices.why: iħ is the commutator of position and momentum. For L̂_x and L̂_y it is iħL̂_z.

explanation: The components of angular momentum do not commute: [L̂_x, L̂_y] = iħL̂_z, [L̂_y, L̂_z] = iħL̂_x and [L̂_z, L̂_x] = iħL̂_y. So no two components can be known exactly at the same time.
